input: When measurements are being discussed, the concept of error is one that frequently arises, and it is helpful to understand clearly what is meant by the term and how it can be expressed. Essentially, the error of a measurement can be thought of as the difference between the reading that is obtained and the true value that the reading is intended to represent. This difference can be expressed in two main ways. The absolute error is simply the magnitude of the difference, expressed in the same units as the measurement itself, whereas the relative error is obtained by dividing the absolute error by the reading, and is commonly expressed as a percentage of the reading. To illustrate these ideas, it is useful to consider a simple flow measurement example. Suppose that a reading of 319 units has been obtained, and that the applicable tolerance is 2% of reading. On this basis, the absolute error amounts to 2% of 319 units, which works out to 6.38 units. It is also important to appreciate the distinction between error and uncertainty, two terms that are sometimes used rather loosely as though they were interchangeable. In fact, they are not the same thing at all: error relates to a specific reading and the difference between that reading and the underlying value, while uncertainty is a broader concept that is concerned with the range within which the value might reasonably be expected to lie, taking into account the instrument and the method that have been used. Keeping these two concepts separate helps to ensure that measurement results are interpreted correctly and communicated clearly.
target:
A measurement error is the difference between a reading and the value that the reading stands for. The error is a property of a single reading: the instrument gives one number, the quantity has one value, and the error is the gap between them. Error is stated in two forms. The absolute error is the size of the difference, in the units of the measurement itself. The relative error is the absolute error divided by the reading, and is a pure ratio, often written as a percentage of the reading. The two forms answer different questions. The absolute error states how far the reading may be out on the scale in use; the relative error states how large that deviation is against the size of the quantity measured, and relative errors can be compared across instruments and scales where absolute errors cannot.

A flow measurement makes the distinction concrete. A reading of 319 units carries a tolerance of 2% of reading. The absolute error is 2% of 319 units, which is 6.38 units. The tolerance grows with the reading, because a percentage of reading is being applied: the same instrument at a larger flow would carry a larger absolute error at the same relative error, and at a smaller flow a smaller one. A tolerance stated as a percentage of reading therefore fixes the relative error and lets the absolute error follow the reading.

Error is not uncertainty. Error attaches to a particular reading as the difference between that reading and the value behind it, a value that is in practice unknown, which is why error is estimated from a tolerance rather than observed directly. Uncertainty describes the measurement as a whole: it states the range within which the value may lie, given the instrument and the method, and it can be attached to a procedure before any single reading is taken. The two terms are not merged here. The worked figure is an error, computed from a stated tolerance on a stated reading, and it makes no claim about the range that an uncertainty statement would give.
